Before the US I taught in Cebu, that's where I'm from, Cebu City in the Philippines. My first teaching job was at Colegio de Santa Lucia, it's a private Catholic school, kindergarten through grade 12, not huge but not small either. I was there two school years. I graduated from the University of San Lorenzo with my Bachelor of Secondary Education, major in biological science, and I passed the licensure exam for teachers, the LET, and then I started at Santa Lucia right away. So that was 2016 to 2018, two school years, and then I flew out to the US in July 2018 for the exchange program.

I taught Grade 7 and Grade 8 science. Five sections, around 45 students each, so honestly more than 200 kids a day, which is normal there. In the Philippines science is spiral, so Grade 7 is a little bit of everything, chemistry, biology, physics, earth science, every quarter a different one. That actually helped me a lot later, because I'd taught every strand at least once.

The thing I remember most is we didn't have a real lab. We had one room with some old equipment and the microscopes were, I think, from the 90s, and half of them didn't focus. So I made lab kits. I'd collect plastic bottles, straws, rubber bands, baking soda, vinegar, stuff from the market, and build kits in shoeboxes, one per group of five. I made maybe 20 different kits over the two years. Density columns, simple circuits with batteries and little bulbs, a bottle rocket one that the kids loved. The other science teachers started borrowing them, and then the department head asked me to write up instructions for each kit so anyone could use them. That was my first time really writing curriculum for other teachers, now that I think about it. I wrote it all up in a binder, with the steps, the safety notes, the questions for the kids. I think they still use the binder. I hope so.

I also ran the school science fair in my second year. Before that it was kind of just posters, and I changed it so the kids had to actually do an investigation with a question and data, and I made a rubric for the judges. We had about 60 projects. Two of our students went on to the division-level fair and one placed, I think third, in the life science category, a project about mosquito larvae and different water samples. Honestly that was probably the best thing that happened there, for the kids.

The pay was very low, that's just the truth for private school teachers there, and that was part of why I applied to the exchange program. The other part was I wanted to see how science was taught somewhere else. A teacher I knew had gone to Nevada with the same sponsor and she said it was hard but worth it.

Leaving was hard. My mom cried at the airport, I cried on the plane. I'd never lived anywhere but Cebu. Then I landed in Las Vegas in July and it was like 110 degrees and I thought, what did I do.

Oh, and the language thing. At Santa Lucia we taught science in English, that's the policy, but with the kids I'd explain in Cebuano when they were lost, and that's something I still do with my English learners here, just in Spanish now, my Spanish is okay, not great. Code-switching to explain a hard idea, I think that's a real skill and I learned it in Cebu.

What I'd say about Santa Lucia overall is it taught me to make something out of nothing. No budget, no lab, 45 kids, figure it out. I think that's why the remote teaching thing in 2020 didn't scare me as much as some people.

I'm also still in touch with some of the teachers there. I've sent them some of my Canvas units, adapted, they don't have Canvas but they print them.
